# Multiparameter Quantitative Analyses of Diagnostic Cells in Brain Tissues from Tuberous Sclerosis Complex

**Authors:** Jerome S. Arceneaux; Asa A. Brockman; Rohit Khurana; Mary-Bronwen L. Chalkley; Laura C. Geben; Aleksandar Krbanjevic; Matthew Vestal; Muhammad Zafar; Sarah Weatherspoon; Bret C. Mobley; Kevin C. Ess; Rebecca A. Ihrie

**Affiliations:** 1Department of Biochemistry, Cancer Biology, Neuroscience, and Pharmacology, Meharry Medical College | 2Department of Cell & Developmental Biology, Vanderbilt University | 3Department of Pharmacology, Vanderbilt University | 4Department of Pathology, Microbiology, & Immunology, Vanderbilt University Medical Center | 5Duke University Children’s Hospital and Health Center | 6Neuroscience Institute, Le Bonheur Children’s Hospital | 7University of Tennessee Health Science Center | 8Department of Pediatrics, Vanderbilt University Medical Center | 9Department of Neurology, Vanderbilt University Medical Center | 10Department of Neurological Surgery, Vanderbilt University Medical Center | 11Section of Child Neurology, University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Center

## Abstract

The advent of high-dimensional imaging offers new opportunities to molecularly characterize diagnostic cells in disorders that have previously relied on histopathological definitions. One example case is found in tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), a developmental disorder characterized by systemic growth of benign tumors. Within resected brain tissues from patients with TSC, detection of abnormally enlarged balloon cells (BCs) is pathognomonic for this disorder. Though BCs can be identified by an expert neuropathologist, little is known about the specificity and broad applicability of protein markers for these cells, complicating classification of proposed BCs identified in experimental models of this disorder. Here, we report the development of a customized machine-learning pipeline (Balloon Identifier; BAIDEN) that was trained to prospectively identify BCs in tissue sections using a histological stain compatible with high-dimensional cytometry. This approach was coupled to a custom 36-antibody panel and imaging mass cytometry (IMC) to explore the expression of multiple previously proposed BC marker proteins and develop a descriptor of BC features conserved across multiple tissue samples from patients with TSC. Here, we present a modular workflow encompassing BAIDEN, a custom antibody panel, a control sample microarray, and analysis pipelines – both open-source and in-house – and apply this workflow to understand the abundance, structure, and signaling activity of BCs as an example case of how high-dimensional imaging can be applied within human tissues.

## Introduction

The advent of high-dimensional approaches for studying fixed tissue specimens, including spatial transcriptomics and multiparameter imaging cytometry (e.g., CODEX, MIBI, and IMC), has greatly expanded opportunities to perform detailed molecular analyses of cell populations that were previously identified using morphological features (Chang et al., 2017; Nowicka et al., 2017; Keren et al., 2019; Black et al., 2021; Brockman et al., 2021; Karimi et al., 2023). Imaging mass cytometry (IMC) is an antibody-based approach that uses time-of-flight mass spectrometry to detect antibodies conjugated to unique heavy metals, enabling simultaneous visualization of 30+ proteins while preserving spatial relationships within the tissue and avoiding the autofluorescence often seen in preserved tissues including brain tissue (reviewed in (Chang et al., 2017; Baharlou et al., 2019; Le Rochais et al., 2022; Glasson et al., 2023) and referenced in (Clancy and Cauller, 1998; Pyon et al., 2019; Zhang et al., 2022; Cords et al., 2023; Fischer et al., 2023; Hiltbrunner et al., 2023; Hosogane et al., 2023; Karimi et al., 2023; Lu et al., 2023; Wang et al., 2023; Cords et al., 2024)). IMC typically focuses on smaller regions of interest (ROIs) on the scale of 1 to 2 square millimeters, but this can be a challenge when the cell population of interest is rare or sparsely spread across a tissue specimen with a size of hundreds of square millimeters. As patient-derived models also expand in scope and complexity, a related question is how best to quantitatively compare unusual cell phenotypes present in these systems to the patient tissues they are intended to model. One tissue where many such models have been developed is the brain, with a particular emphasis on developmental or genetic disorders that are studied using models such as cerebral organoids (Lancaster et al., 2013; Blair et al., 2018; Sloan et al., 2018; Eichmuller et al., 2022).

Focal cortical dysplasias (FCDs) are neurodevelopmental disorders characterized by disorganization of the cerebral cortex, including altered lamination and the presence of multiple dysmorphic cells; these disorders have an incidence of 1 in 2000 live births annually (Neligan and Sander, 2011; Crino, 2015; Blumcke et al., 2017; Blumcke et al., 2021a; Blumcke et al., 2021b). Nearly two-thirds of individuals with FCD have intractable epilepsy, and FCDs account for about 17% of the pediatric surgical population, underscoring an urgent medical need for therapeutic targets (Thiele, 2010; Crino, 2015; Baldassari et al., 2019). Nearly all identified causative mutations for FCDs (~90%) affect proteins interacting with or within the mammalian / mechanistic target of rapamycin (mTOR) pathway, a central regulator of cell size and growth (Lipton and Sahin, 2014; Crino, 2016; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017; Baldassari et al., 2019). Currently, FCDs associated with mutations in mTOR pathway-associated proteins other than TSC1 (hamartin) or TSC2 (tuberin) are categorized as non-TSC-associated FCDs; this class includes mutations in MTOR, AKT, RHEB, DEPDC5, PTEN, and PIK3CA (Baulac et al., 2015; D’Gama et al., 2017; Ribierre et al., 2018; Baldassari et al., 2019). Heterozygous mutations in either TSC1 or TSC2 are categorized as TSC-associated FCD and are found in patients with tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC), an autosomal dominant disorder (Camposano et al., 2009; Crino, 2013; Baldassari et al., 2019). TSC affects about 1 in 6000 live births annually and is characterized by the growth of benign tumors, also termed hamartomas, in many organs including the brain (Zimmer et al., 2020). Patients exhibit multiple neurological symptoms, including epilepsy, cognitive impairment or developmental delay, autism spectrum disorder (ASD), and TSC-associated neuropsychiatric disorders (TANDs) (Barkovich et al., 2015; De Vries et al., 2015).

At the cellular level, TSC-associated FCD is distinguished by the presence of balloon cells (BCs), atypical cells identified by an enlarged, ovoid soma and an eccentrically placed nucleus (Urbach et al., 2002; Lamparello et al., 2007; Crino, 2013). Though these cells are a diagnostic feature of TSC, their possible origins and properties have been relatively unexplored until the advent of mouse models and patient-derived in vitro models (e.g., cerebral organoids). Multiple such models have been reported to contain abnormal cells that histologically resemble BCs; however, the molecular profile of BCs in patient tissues has not been systematically described, complicating such comparisons (Li et al., 2017; Blair et al., 2018; Eichmuller et al., 2022; Karalis et al., 2022; Kovermann et al., 2022; Wu et al., 2022). In prior studies of patient tissues, many proteins have been postulated to selectively identify BCs, including proteins associated with progenitor cells, mature neuronal and glial cells, and phosphorylation events driven by mTOR kinase activity (Hilbig et al., 1999; Mizuguchi et al., 2002; Urbach et al., 2002; Ying et al., 2005; Lamparello et al., 2007; Orlova et al., 2010; Yasin et al., 2010; Ruppe et al., 2014; Rossini et al., 2017; Gelot and Represa, 2020). However, these studies used single- or double-channel immunohistochemistry, limiting the ability to identify coexpression patterns, and it is not yet clear how uniformly any given protein is expressed in BCs across either individual tubers or patient cohorts (Urbach et al., 2002; Palmini et al., 2004; Najm et al., 2022).

An additional factor limiting efforts to study BCs in the numbers needed for statistically robust descriptions is the challenge of manually identifying these cells in a large, resected sample of hundreds of square millimeters, which can be a laborious and time-intensive process. This study introduces a trainable, machine-learning tool to efficiently identify BCs from whole-slide images, allowing for the rapid identification of fields with a sufficient number of localized BCs for deeper study with imaging mass cytometry (IMC). A custom antibody panel was developed in parallel to simultaneously quantify 30+ protein species of interest. Using this approach across tissue sections from multiple TSC patients, we found that BCs express progenitor proteins while selectively lacking proteins of differentiated progeny and display heightened mTORC1-dependent activity. We also observed sample-to-sample variation in enrichment for several previously proposed BC proteins, suggesting that the reported mixed-lineage phenotype of these cells is variable across patients. This study illustrates the utility of high-dimensional, protein-based imaging in better understanding possible and consistent features of diagnostic cells in human tissues.

## Materials & Methods

### Human Specimens and Tissue Processing

Tissues were collected from Vanderbilt Children’s Hospital between 2018 and 2023 under IRB #130550, from Duke University Hospital in 2022 under IRB #108389, and from Le Bonheur Children’s Hospital between 2022 and 2023 under IRB #20-07761-XP with written informed consent in accordance with the Declaration of Helsinki. Samples were deidentified before processing. A complete list of patient demographics and clinical characteristics, as well as which samples were used for which approaches, can be found in Table 3. Tubers and perituberal tissues were obtained within 1 hour of resection. Samples were processed into slabs of tissue 5-10 mm thick and placed in 10% neutral buffered formalin (Fisher Scientific; 426-796) for 24-36 hours at 4°C prior to transfer to 70% ethanol. Processing into paraffin, serial sectioning of samples, and standard hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining were performed by the Translational Pathology Shared Resource (TPSR) at Vanderbilt University Medical Center.

Two specimens (VUT021 and VUT036) were used to train and test BAIDEN (see BAIDEN below) while 8 specimens (DUH01, DUH02I, LBH002-2, VUT021, VUT022, VUT034, VUT036, and VUT037) were imaged by imaging mass cytometry (IMC). Of the 8 specimens imaged, 5 specimens (DUH01, DUH02I, LBH002-2, VUT034, and VUT037) were included in downstream analyses.

### Metal-Tagged Antibody In-House Conjugations

All antibodies used for IMC analysis are listed in Table 1. Custom-conjugated antibodies (shown in bold text in Table 1) were prepared using standard methods with Maxpar X8® Chelating Polymer Kits (Standard BioTools; 201300) (Bendall et al., 2011). Each antibody clone was validated using known positive and negative control samples in the microarray described next.

### Control Sample Microarray Design and Construction

For each antibody, identified positive and negative control samples were selected by consulting the scientific literature and resources, including the Human Protein Atlas (www.proteinatlas.org) (Uhlén et al., 2015). For example, for phosphorylated proteins, positive control cell pellets for the microarray were generated by stimulating live cells in suspension with specific cytokines known to induce phosphorylation on a time scale of minutes (Irish et al., 2004). Similarly, for phosphorylation events that are normally high in cancer cell lines, negative controls were generated by sustained treatment of live cells with small-molecule inhibitors (e.g., rapamycin for inhibition of mTOR phosphorylation of S6). Following rapid fixation with 1.6% electron microscopy (EM)-grade paraformaldehyde, a portion of the untreated and treated cells were collected for flow cytometry measurement of phospho-proteins while the remainder of the cells were transferred to 70% ethanol and formed into a pellet for paraffinization. Cell pellets and selected tissue samples were then used to construct the custom control sample microarray (microarray preparation from shipped samples completed at Acepix Biosciences). Slide-mounted sections of the paraffin-embedded control sample microarray were then prepared by TPSR in parallel with the tuber tissues described above. The full list of 21 positive and negative control samples can be found in Table 2.

### Epitope Retrieval and Slide Processing

Slides were deparaffinized, rehydrated, and subjected to heat-induced epitope retrieval using Trilogy (Sigma-Aldrich; 920P-09) in a Cuisinart pressure cooker following the manufacturer’s directions and published protocols (Faolain et al., 2005; Krenacs et al., 2010; Catena et al., 2018). Slides were incubated at a high-pressure setting for 10 minutes in a 50-mL Coplin jar, followed by manual pressure release (approximately 3 minutes) and a 5-minute rinse in a second 50-mL Coplin jar of Trilogy that was heated in the pressure cooker and allowed to cool during rinsing (termed “hot rinse”). Slides were then rinsed for 5 minutes with room temperature ddH2O.

For paraffin-dipped slides, to ensure complete paraffin removal, individual slides were 1) dewaxed in separate Coplin jars with 2 xylene washes for 30 minutes each at room temperature in a chemical fume hood; 2) deparaffinized, rehydrated, and subjected to heat-induced epitope retrieval for 10 minutes in a Cuisinart pressure cooker with Trilogy as described above, using a separate Coplin jar for each slide; 3) and underwent two Trilogy “hot rinses” for 5 minutes each (Krenacs et al., 2010; Shi et al., 2011; Metgud et al., 2013; Hughes et al., 2014; Gaifulina et al., 2020; Zaqout et al., 2020; Smart et al., 2023). Slides were then rinsed for 5 minutes with room temperature ddH2O.

### Toluidine Blue O Incubation and Imaging

Following dewaxing and epitope retrieval, slides were prepared for toluidine blue O (TBO; Sigma-Aldrich; T3260) staining in a Parhelia OmniStainer as described below (Parhelia Biosciences; 40002). After 3 x 5-minute rinses in 1X PBS, samples were incubated with 1% TBO (w/v) for 5 minutes at room temperature. Samples were rinsed for 5 minutes with 1X PBS and removed from the Parhelia OmniStainer, and coverslips were mounted with aqueous mounting media (1:1 1X PBS:glycerol), and covered and mounted slides were used for whole-slide, 40X brightfield imaging on a Zeiss Axioscan 7 whole-slide scanner (Neurovisualization Lab at Vanderbilt University).

### BAIDEN

Balloon Identifier (BAIDEN; https://github.com/ihrie-lab/BAIDEN) is a pixel-based classifier that identifies balloon cells (BCs) from input whole-slide images of tuber specimens stained with toluidine blue O (TBO). BAIDEN operates at the image tile level and stitches together its outputs to form a new multi-channel, whole-slide image composed of the original TBO stain, the model’s BC probability estimates, and a second copy of the TBO-stained image in which identified BCs are outlined in red (also detailed below). The underlying model was developed using ilastik, a machine-learning toolkit that uses random forests to estimate segmentation masks based on pixel-level features related to color and intensity, edges, and texture (Berg et al., 2019).

After probabilistically estimating the occurrence of BCs, BAIDEN feeds the generated segmented maps into CellProfiler for finer object detection (Carpenter et al., 2006). In a sequential fashion, the outputs from ilastik are smoothed with a Gaussian kernel (σ = 1) and subjected to primary object identification in which red outlines are constructed around the most likely BCs with the appropriate, user-defined diameter (between 15 and 100 pixels). These outlines are then overlaid onto the original TBO image to ease visualization of identified BCs for downstream region of interest (ROI) identification for imaging mass cytometry (IMC).

### Immunostaining for Imaging Mass Cytometry

#### Blocking Solution

The blocking solution for all immunostaining approaches was 1X PBS (no Ca2+ / Mg2+) with 1% normal donkey serum (Fisher Scientific; OB003001), 1% bovine serum albumin (Sigma-Aldrich; A7906), 0.1% Triton X-100 (Fisher Scientific; AAA16046AE), and 0.01% sodium azide (Fisher Scientific; BP922I) as a preservative. The blocking solution was stored at 4°C between uses.

### Blocking and Antibody Incubation in Parhelia OmniStainer and Imaging Mass Cytometry

Following TBO staining and imaging, coverslips and mounting media were soaked off in water, and the slides were placed in a Parhelia OmniStainer. An OmniStainer covertile (Parhelia Biosciences; 40201) was applied, creating a capillary channel for application of staining solutions, and slides were rinsed one time each with ddH2O, 1X PBS, and blocking solution in sequence. Fresh blocking solution was added and incubated for 30 minutes at room temperature. Metal-tagged antibodies diluted in blocking solution were applied as described above and incubated overnight at 4°C. The following day, samples were rinsed 3 x 5 minutes with 1X PBS and 1 x 5 minutes with ddH2O. The covertile was removed, and slides were allowed to dry overnight before running IMC with a Hyperion™ Imaging System (Standard BioTools) in the Human Immunology Core at Washington University in St. Louis. Tissue was ablated with a UV laser at 200 Hz, ion counts were recorded and mapped to pixel locations using the CyTOF software (version 7.0.8493), and data were exported as .mcd and .txt files as previously reported (Lu et al., 2023).

### Image Processing for Display

#### Raw Image Export

Images from the Hyperion™ Imaging System were exported as single-channel TIFFs for further processing using histoCAT++ (https://github.com/BodenmillerGroup/histoCAT3D). Images acquired as part of IMC included brightfield, whole-slide scans of the full specimen, enabling alignment with previously acquired TBO images, image tiles with per-pixel ion counts for each mass-tagged antibody channel in the field selected for ablation, and brightfield images of those fields pre- and post-laser ablation.

#### Spillover Correction (Data Acquisition and Application)

To account for any isotopic impurities in metals or spillover of signal between channels, a spillover matrix (SM) slide (Supplemental Table 1) was generated and analyzed according to open-source instructions (https://bodenmillergroup.github.io/steinbock/latest/) and as previously reported (Chevrier et al., 2018). The CATALYST package in R was used to import the individual .txt files for each spotted, metal-tagged antibody, create and apply the SM, and export the SM as a .csv and the spillover-corrected channels as stacked TIFFs for each imaged ROI (Nowicka et al., 2017).

#### Arcsinh Transformation and Cofactor Application

To ensure each channel exhibited protein expression and localization consistent with previous validation data, each control sample was critically examined and compared with in-house, fluorescence-based imaging (data not shown) and a published reference atlas (Human Protein Atlas; https://www.proteinatlas.org/) (Uhlén et al., 2015). To best separate signal and noise using known positive and negative control samples (Figures S2 and S3; Table 2), an in-house Python script processed raw images and transformed the images with an inverse hyperbolic sine (arcsinh) function, using expert-selected cofactors for each metal-tagged antibody (Table 1). These cofactors were applied prior to the Python, histoCAT++, and steinbock analyses discussed below.

#### Image Registration

IMC images were registered with brightfield TBO images by isolating the approximate area imaged by IMC within the brightfield slide scan through consultation of an annotated thumbnail image depicting the imaged region by IMC. The resolution of the brightfield TBO image was reduced to match the resolution of the IMC image using ImageJ / FIJI (https://fiji.sc/), with the size transformation calculated using the per-pixel scale of each image. A pixel-to-pixel registration between the individual tiled TBO and IMC images was then achieved using the histone H3 (HH3) IMC channel overlayed onto the downscaled, brightfield TBO image. Rigid registration was sufficient to achieve near-pixel-perfect registration across the imaged ROI. Adjacent H&E was manually registered to TBO by aligning tissue edges and macroscopic features in ImageJ / FIJI.

### IMC Data Analysis

#### steinbock Processing and Export

Raw .mcd files were processed by steinbock as the Docker container according to open-source instructions (https://bodenmillergroup.github.io/steinbock/latest/) and as previously reported (Windhager et al., 2023). Briefly, command-line usage was used to classify pixels as either nucleus, cytoplasm, or background and produce a probability map (ilastik); segment individual cells according to the probability map produced from ilastik and produce cell masks (CellProfiler); measure mean mass intensities (MMIs) from each identified cell according to the cell masks from CellProfiler; and export .csv files (Carpenter et al., 2006; Berg et al., 2019).

#### Image Annotation

An expert neuropathologist viewed stacked images of H&E, TBO, HH3, and p-S6S240 / S244 and annotated probable BCs using the ‘MultiPoint’ tool in ImageJ / FIJI.

### Statistical Analysis

Statistical analysis was performed in R version 4.3.1, GraphPad Prism version 10.1.1, or Python version 3.10.4, where indicated. All analyses were graphed in R, Prism, or Python. Interrater reliability for BCs was calculated as previously reported (McHugh, 2012). Briefly, an expert neuropathologist (B.C.M.) and 4 additional independent raters (2 cell biologists [R.A.I., A.A.B.], 1 neurologist [K.C.E.], and 1 additional pathologist [A.K.]) manually identified BCs using H&E images. After each rater had manually identified BCs in each training image, each identified BC in each training image was given a number, and each rater’s identification of the numbered BCs was determined for congruence by a separate individual (J.S.A).

Statistical analysis of aggregated, individual BCs and non-BCs from different patient samples was performed using a two-tailed, Mann-Whitney test. Bonferroni correction was applied, resulting in a p-value significance cutoff of 0.002 for the violin plots. Statistical analysis of paired BCs and non-BCs from different patient samples was performed using a two-tailed, Mann-Whitney test. Bonferroni correction was applied, resulting in a p-value significance cutoff of 0.0003 for summary Tukey box-and-whisker plots. Unless otherwise indicated, p-values less than 0.05 were considered significant for all statistical tests.

The marker enrichment scores of BCs and non-BCs were identified per sample using the MEM package in R, where MEM labels were generated using all proteins included in Table 1, except CD29 (integrin β1), PTPRZ1, and p-STAT5Y694, which were removed during quality control checks. The display threshold for MEM labels was set at an exponent of ±2 (Diggins et al., 2017).

## Results

### Balloon Identifier (BAIDEN) can be trained to identify balloon cells in tubers.

As an initial-use case for the semi-automated identification of unusual cells based on histopathological criteria, we tested the ability of a trainable, machine-learning pipeline to identify the enlarged balloon cells (BCs) found in brain tissue from patients with TSC (Figures 1, 2, and S2). Traditionally, BCs are identified in resected epileptic foci from patients using hematoxylin and eosin (H&E) staining, which is not yet readily compatible with high-dimensional approaches such as imaging mass cytometry (IMC). BCs are often present at extremely low abundance within a given tissue (1% or less of total cells), complicating efforts to select focused regions of interest (ROIs) for high-dimensional studies. Toluidine blue O (TBO), which has a high affinity for acidic tissue components, including nucleic acids, can be combined with IMC (Sridharan and Shankar, 2012; Baars et al., 2021). Therefore, a Balloon Identifier (BAIDEN) workflow was established to automate the identification of prospective BCs, to identify ROIs with high densities of such cells, and to scale these processes across the large areas included in whole-slide images (Figures 1 and 2A; https://github.com/ihrie-lab/BAIDEN).

Tuber samples obtained during resections of epileptic foci from 2 separate patients were processed into paraffin, sectioned, and stained with TBO prior to collection of whole-slide images. Following imaging of TBO, the same slides were processed for H&E staining, whole-slide images were collected, and the resulting paired TBO-H&E images were registered and tiled. Completion of the BAIDEN workflow generated reconstructed whole-slide images with the following 4 channels: H&E, TBO alone, a grayscale probability mask identifying possible BCs, and a TBO image on which cells exceeding a user-defined, probability threshold was identified and outlined. The workflow was trained using an initial set of 20 tiles from these whole-slide images, each 1.18 mm x 1.18 mm taken at 20X magnification, in which an expert neuropathologist (B.C.M.) and 4 additional independent raters (2 cell biologists [R.A.I., A.A.B.], 1 neurologist [K.C.E.], and 1 additional pathologist [A.K.]) manually identified BCs using H&E images. The training images were curated from a larger set of randomly selected tiles to ensure the data captured various BC morphologies, fields with no BCs, and some typical experimental artifacts (e.g., torn or folded tissue). The trained workflow was then applied to a separate testing dataset of 20 additional neuropathologist-annotated tiles to evaluate performance versus an expert alone. In this dataset, BAIDEN achieved a precision of 0.9273 and a recall of 0.6892 versus neuropathologist annotation, indicating that it was highly accurate in outlining 92.73% of “true” BCs but potentially excluded some BCs (31%) that could not be assigned with high confidence (Figure S2). This level of accuracy was comparable to the combined performance of all 5 expert raters, where the observed interrater reliability was 88.6%. The available implementation of BAIDEN allows users to set different thresholds for labeling probable BCs on analyzed images, meaning this parameter could be adjusted if the user preference was to identify all possible BCs while potentially including some false positives (i.e., lowering precision). In this instance, rigorous identification of bona fide BCs was prioritized. Following this initial use on training and testing datasets, BAIDEN was applied to images of tuber tissue to prospectively select ROIs for study using IMC. Following ROI selection, which ranged from 1.0 mm2 to 2.25 mm2 from tissue slices with a total area of 600 to 900 mm2, tuber samples were stained and analyzed by IMC (Figures 1 and 2B).

To systematically explore previously proposed BC markers and lineage features, a customized panel of 36 mass-tagged antibodies was developed in tandem with a microarray of 21 positive and negative control samples – a critical component to identify and minimize possible artifacts and batch effects due to antigen retrieval or antibody cocktail preparation (Figure 3; Figures S3 and S4; Tables 1 and 2). The antibody panel included proteins that distinguish major immature and mature cell types expected to be present in normal brain (GFAP, EAAT1, SMI-311, β-III-tubulin, OLIG2, MBP, CD45, and CD31), proposed BC proteins (EGFR, TTF-1 [NKX2.1], CD133, CD29 [integrin β1], vimentin, FAPB7 [BLBP], and EMX1), and phosphorylated proteins indicative of elevated mTOR kinase activity (p-S6S240 / S244, p4EBP1T37 / T46, and p-STAT3S727) and overlapping signaling pathways (MAPK, RSK, and EGFR). The microarray samples included positive and negative control samples for each antigen – either with tissues where the expression pattern is well-documented for total proteins or with pharmacologically manipulated cell lines for each phosphorylation event of interest (e.g., cells with high basal p-S6 levels untreated or treated with the known mTOR kinase inhibitor rapamycin). In all cases, the expected pattern of signal for a given antigen was confirmed using an orthogonal approach (fluorescent or colorimetric immunostaining, Western blotting, and / or flow cytometry). For each protein of interest, the range and specificity of signal intensity across all control microarray samples were used to confirm successful staining when processed alongside tissue samples (Figure 3; Figures S3 and S4). Based on these initial quality-control assessments, three antigens (CD29 [integrin β1], PTPRZ1, and p-STAT5Y694) were removed from further analyses, as they did not reliably exhibit staining in positive controls or other samples.

### Balloon cells in tubers are cytomegalic and variably abundant.

A set of 8 resected tuber samples was stained using the IMC panel detailed above (Table 1). Prior to ablation for mass-based imaging, each sample was stained with TBO to enable prospective identification of BCs via BAIDEN, and an adjacent serial section was stained with H&E (Figure 4) to aid in confirmatory manual, retrospective annotation. Candidate BC-containing ROIs were first identified by running BAIDEN on whole-slide images, and the full slide was then stained with the IMC antibody panel prior to laser ablation and collection of ion counts in the specific ROIs identified using BAIDEN. These ROIs were also retrospectively annotated for confirmed BCs by an expert neuropathologist (B.C.M.) using aligned TBO, H&E, histone H3 (HH3), and p-S6S240 / S244 mass cytometry channels (Figures 1 and 4A). Images with BAIDEN- and expert-annotated BCs were subsequently processed to analyze all mass-tagged antibody channels using the steinbock pipeline (Windhager et al., 2023). Across the 8 tissue samples, 197 BCs were identified out of 16,942 cells (1.16%). The highest number of BCs identified in a tissue was 60 in an area of 1.5 mm2 (DUH01; 4.86%) while the lowest number was 0 in an area of 1.0 mm2 (VUT036). 3 of the 8 tissues (VUT021, VUT022, and VUT036) were excluded from downstream analyses as they contained fewer than 5 identified BCs in the imaged ROIs. A total of 192 BCs out of 12,725 cells (1.51%) was used for downstream analyses (Figure S6), and the largest area imaged was 2.25 mm2 (LBH002-2 and VUT034; Table 3). To support the goal of identifying proteins selectively enriched in BCs versus all other cells present in the tissue, signal intensity for each protein, as well as a subset of scored cytoarchitectural features, was compared between BCs and non-BCs (Figures 4 and 5; Figures S5 and S6). As expected, BCs tended to have a larger area (Figure 5C) and decreased eccentricity (Figure S6) relative to other cells within tuber samples. While BCs in some samples were enriched for specific features, a relatively limited number of proteins showed consistent increases in BCs versus matched non-BCs when compared across all analyzed samples (Figures S5 and S6).

### Balloon cells show elevated mTOR-dependent phosphorylation events.

Consistent with previous reports, BCs exhibited higher per-cell levels of protein phosphorylation events associated with mTOR kinase activity. Sample-to-sample variability was observed for specific phospho-proteins, with BCs in 3 out of 5 tissues having statistically significant elevated levels of mTOR complex 1 (mTORC1) effectors p-S6S240 / S244, p-S6S235 / S236, p-4EBP1T37 / T46, and p-STAT3S727 (Figure S5). BCs in 3 of 5 samples showed increased levels of p-STAT3Y705 (Figure S5). There was no reproducible change in other readouts, including p-AKTS473 and p-NDRG1T346 (Figures S5 and S6), which are more closely associated with mTOR complex 2 (mTORC2) activation (Schreiber et al., 2015; Szwed et al., 2021). BCs in 3 of 5 tissues had increased levels of p-ERK1/2T202 / Y204 while BCs in 1 tissue had decreased levels of p-ERK1/2T202 / Y204 (Figure S5). Similarly, we did not reliably observe differences in per-cell levels of TFEB (Figure S5), which changes localization upon phosphorylation by mTOR (Alesi et al., 2021; Alesi et al., 2024). To complement per-sample comparisons, we pooled all BCs and non-BCs from the 5 studied samples and tested for significant differences in staining intensity for the proteins of interest. When aggregated across samples, BCs showed increased levels of p-S6S240 / S244, p-S6S235 / S236, p-4EBP1T37 / T46, p-STAT3S727, and p-STAT3Y705 (Figure 4E).

### Balloon cells variably express progenitor-associated proteins.

Multiple proteins and posttranslational protein modifications have been proposed to selectively identify BCs, ranging from those associated more strongly with progenitor lineages to those used to distinguish mature-cell types within the adult brain (Hilbig et al., 1999; Mizuguchi et al., 2002; Urbach et al., 2002; Ying et al., 2005; Lamparello et al., 2007; Orlova et al., 2010; Yasin et al., 2010; Ruppe et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017; Rossini et al., 2017; Gelot and Represa, 2020; Wu et al., 2022). BCs across all tissues had decreased expression of β-III-tubulin at both the per-sample level and when aggregated, and 3 of 5 samples showed decreased expression of SMI-311 when compared on a per-sample basis but not when aggregated (Figures S5 and S6). BCs, when compared on a per-sample basis, tended to show decreased levels of astrocytic proteins GFAP and EAAT1 but did not show significant differences in the aggregate (Figures S5 and S6). 2 of 5 samples showed decreased MBP in BCs, though this difference was not significant when examined in the aggregate (Figures S5 and S6). BCs showed increased expression of vimentin across 4 of 5 samples (Figure S5) and in the aggregate, as did CD133 (Figure 5C). SOX2, a transcription factor expressed in progenitor and mature cell types, was enriched in all per-sample comparisons and in the aggregate (Figures 5C and S5). In contrast, the progenitor protein FABP7 was enriched in 2 of 5 per-sample comparisons (Figure S5) but not in the aggregate (Figure S6). BCs also showed slightly increased expression of TTF-1, EMX1, EGFR, DCX, GAD67, and OLIG2 (Figure 5C). BCs showed decreased expression of β-III-tubulin across 3 of 5 tissues and in the aggregate (Figures 5D, S5).

### A statistical description of BC-enriched features.

To identify potential BC descriptors that were conserved across cells in all 5 samples and produce a statistical label that could be used in future cross-platform analyses, the marker enrichment modeling (MEM) statistic was used to identify proteins that were selectively enriched or selectively de-enriched when BCs were compared to the remainder of the tissue (Diggins et al., 2017). Of the parameters measured, vimentin and p-S6S240 / S244 were reliably enriched (positive MEM label and exponent) in BCs versus matched non-BCs across samples (Figure 5D). Consistent with single-channel comparisons above, some samples also displayed enrichment or de-enrichment for additional proteins in BCs versus other cells in the tissue (Figure 5D).

## Discussion

There is widespread interest in working with patient samples to identify therapeutic targets, especially for rare diseases with limited treatment options such as tuberous sclerosis complex (TSC). In TSC, identification of balloon cells (BCs) is pathognomonic, yet BCs can vary widely in abundance both within and across surgically resected tissue sections and patients – in this study, the percentage of BCs in analyzed fields ranged from 0.14% to 4.86%, with many other fields not selected for IMC containing no BCs, and each specimen requiring hundreds of fields for a comprehensive view at suitable magnification. Currently, the “gold standard” for identifying BCs relies on expert annotation by a neuropathologist using cytoarchitectural features (Urbach et al., 2002; Becker et al., 2006; Blumcke et al., 2011; Blumcke et al., 2017; Blumcke et al., 2021b). However, this process can be time-consuming and may introduce interrater variability. A further challenge is the comparison of abnormal cells found in organoid or mouse models of TSC to bona fide BCs, including the ability to distinguish plausible BCs from the dysmorphic neurons that can also be found in tissues of patients with TSC and related disorders, emphasizing the need to increase the efficiency and rapidity of identifying BCs.

We developed a trainable, machine-learning approach to efficiently identify BCs from whole-slide images stained with a colorimetric stain. Though the patient samples used in this study were cortical tissues from TSC patients, BAIDEN can be trained and tested on any tissue type or disorder, given sufficient depth in the training data to distinguish the cells of interest. One critical feature of its use is that the training, testing, and analysis datasets must be as uniform as possible in the staining protocol used for toluidine blue O (TBO) or other equivalent stains. While probable BCs could still be highlighted in the experimental samples described here, the probability threshold (i.e., the level of certainty when identifying probable BCs) was lower when staining or image quality was affected by experimental variation. In the future, it will be of interest to re-train BAIDEN and other approaches with additional parameters collected from these studies (e.g., vimentin, p-S6S240 / S244, cell size, and eccentricity) to test whether including these additional features can improve the reliable identification of BCs and the neuropathological diagnosis of TSC. Moreover, it will be intriguing to determine if this approach can be extended to rapidly identify cells of interest for applications such as laser-capture microdissection, which has been used to address the question of whether TSC1/2 loss of heterozygosity (LOH) occurs in BCs and / or other cells found within epileptic foci (Ichikawa et al., 2005; Giannikou et al., 2016; Bongaarts et al., 2017; D’Gama et al., 2017; Blair et al., 2018; Baldassari et al., 2019; Eichmuller et al., 2022).

Histopathologically, BCs are characterized by an enlarged, ovoid soma and an eccentrically placed nucleus (Urbach et al., 2002; Lamparello et al., 2007; Saxton and Sabatini, 2017; Najm et al., 2022). BCs in the patient tissues analyzed by IMC showed an increased area and were rounder than non-BCs, quantitatively supporting these metrics (Urbach et al., 2002; Becker et al., 2006; Blumcke et al., 2011; Blumcke et al., 2017; Blumcke et al., 2021b). Consistent with previous studies and case reports, BCs in the patient samples had heightened mTORC1-dependent signaling (Hilbig et al., 1999; Mizuguchi et al., 2002; Urbach et al., 2002; Ying et al., 2005; Lamparello et al., 2007; Orlova et al., 2010; Yasin et al., 2010; Ruppe et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017; Rossini et al., 2017; Gelot and Represa, 2020). Both residues of p-S6 – p-S6S240 / S244 and p-S6S235 / S236 – were elevated in some BCs. The S240 / S244 residue is phosphorylated by p70 S6 kinase, a direct target of mTOR, while ribosome S6 kinase (RSK) can also phosphorylate the S235 / S236 residue (Ruvinsky et al., 2005; Ruvinsky and Meyuhas, 2006; Crino, 2013). In addition, both residues of p-STAT3 – p-STAT3S727 and p-STAT3Y705 – were elevated in some BCs. While the S727 residue is primarily phosphorylated by mTOR, the Y705 residue is also phosphorylated by several other kinases and is necessary for the dimerization and transcriptional activity of STAT3 (Huang et al., 2014). The mean mass intensity (MMI) value differences between BCs and non-BCs were more statistically robust for p-S6S240 / S244 and p-STAT3S727, suggesting there is a preference towards mTORC1-dependent phosphorylation, consistent with the slightly elevated levels of p-4EBP1T37 / T46.

As the understanding of BCs as a hallmark of TSC-associated FCD has grown, interest in identifying their cell of origin has increased. Prior work has postulated BCs express various proteins that distinguish progenitor cells and their differentiated progeny, yet these studies largely did not assess these proteins simultaneously nor across multiple samples and patients (Hilbig et al., 1999; Mizuguchi et al., 2002; Urbach et al., 2002; Ying et al., 2005; Lamparello et al., 2007; Orlova et al., 2010; Yasin et al., 2010; Ruppe et al., 2014; Li et al., 2017; Rossini et al., 2017; Gelot and Represa, 2020). BCs in the patient tissues examined here tended to express proteins associated with progenitor cell identity and function rather than mature cell identity and function. Specifically, vimentin, SOX2, CD133, and EGFR were elevated in BCs while proteins used to identify mature cells, including β-III-tubulin, SMI-311, GFAP, and EAAT1, tended to be decreased.

In the developing brain, regional patterning is associated with the generation of specific neuronal subtypes and can be detected via staining for region-specific transcription factors that are expressed at specific developmental stages. TTF-1, which distinguishes the medial ganglionic eminences (ventral structures), has previously been proposed as a protein largely absent from tubers (Rushing et al., 2019). Interestingly, the BCs analyzed by IMC had slightly increased expression of both TTF-1 and the transcription factor EMX1 (typically prevalent in cortex), though this varied across samples. BCs also had increased expression of DCX, which distinguishes migratory immature neurons (Gleeson et al., 1999; Ayanlaja et al., 2017). Collectively, these patterns of expression, as well as the MEM scores for BCs in each sample, suggest that while BCs reflect an immature and / or mixed-lineage phenotype, relatively few proposed proteins distinguishing these cell types are uniformly expressed from cell to cell or patient to patient. Identification of uniform and variable features may help in determining which signaling arms of this pathway can and should be targeted in tubers and BCs – a relevant question as not all mTOR inhibitors in development for the clinic have equivalent efficacy against the same downstream phosphorylation events (Choi et al., 1996; Fan et al., 2018; Mao et al., 2022). As in studies of other progenitor populations, examining multiple parameters will likely be critical to confirming BC, or BC-like, identity in cell-based models. In this regard, the use of MEM labels, a platform-independent statistic that enables cross-platform comparison of phenotypes across samples, will be useful in developing unified standards for this identity.

Some challenges and important considerations were evident in these initial studies. First, though random forest – used in ilastik and, thus, in BAIDEN – is a reliable, well-established algorithm for pixel classification, there are deep-learning algorithms (e.g., U-Net) and segmentation toolkits (e.g., Cellpose and Mesmer) available that may have the potential to further improve automated BC identification (Ronneberger et al., 2015; Stringer et al., 2021; Greenwald et al., 2022). However, these algorithms and toolkits require large, labeled datasets for training (e.g., tens of thousands of annotated images), which are not always readily available for rare diseases, including TSC. As more samples are obtained, it will be important to continue to generate labeled datasets to allow benchmarking of these alternative approaches against BAIDEN and to potentially further improve the performance of BAIDEN itself. Second, xylene washes were used to remove excess paraffin coating on paraffin-dipped slides. Though this approach is used extensively in standard histopathology for paraffin-embedded specimens (e.g., immunohistochemical staining with colorimetric detection) and in spectroscopy-based imaging, for imaging mass cytometry it should be tested for each antigen / antibody combination to ensure reliable identification of antigen of interest following this process, as was done here (Krenacs et al., 2010; Metgud et al., 2013; Hughes et al., 2014; Nallala et al., 2015; Gaifulina et al., 2020; Zaqout et al., 2020; Smart et al., 2023). Furthermore, each protein measured must be critically assessed by comparing against orthogonal approaches (e.g., phospho-flow cytometry or fluorescence immunostaining of samples with no xylene washes) or against standard samples (e.g., a control sample array or the Human Protein Atlas) (Uhlén et al., 2015). Third, despite the uniform preparation and staining of all tissue sections and controls with a single antibody cocktail, we did observe sample-to-sample variation in staining intensity, as evident in per-sample comparisons. This variation could be due to initial fixation and processing for older samples (VUT021, VUT022) and may also reflect regional variation within cortical tissue, as tubers can present in many locations in the brain and display variability in their radiographic and pathologic features (Jesmanas et al., 2018). This final caveat is likely to be relevant for many studies on formalin-fixed, paraffin-embedded samples, especially for rare diseases where samples may be archived for extended periods. Nonetheless, systematic comparisons across tissue samples were able to highlight proteins with uniform direction of variation across patients (i.e., proteins that were always enriched, or always de-enriched, in BCs versus non-BCs). These comparisons could be further refined by systematically identifying suitable normal cell comparators within the tissue of interest. Last, carefully generating standardized control samples for each antibody was essential in identifying the dynamic range of signal for each channel and verifying that xylene and heat-induced epitope retrieval did not destroy antigens of interest, thus, confirming that the lack of signal in cells of interest (as in the case of mature-cell proteins in BCs) was a true negative signal and not loss of antigen from either xylene washes or heat-induced epitope retrieval. Collectively, these data present a panel development, validation, staining, and analysis strategy that can be applied to the brain and many other tissues where high-dimensional imaging is of interest.
